## Introduction

In this assignment, we explore the Seoul Bike Sharing dataset and develop multiple linear regression models to predict daily bicycle rentals.

We begin by importing and exploring the data, then prepare the data for modeling, fit three regression models, and compare their predictive performance using RMSE.

## Reading in the Data

```{r}
# Load the packages needed for data manipulation and exploration
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(rsample)
library(cowplot)

# Read the locally saved Seoul Bike Sharing dataset
# Specify Latin1 encoding to handle special characters
bike_data <- read_csv(
  "data/SeoulBikeData.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "Latin1")
)
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

With the data imported, we conducted a basic EDA, including the following:

```{r}
cate_tables <- bike_data |> # Target only categorical variables

basic_eda
```

* Lastly, rename the all the variables to have easy to use names

```{r}
clean_bikes <- bike_data |>
  # Convert string to a true date obj.
  rename(
    date          = Date,
    bikeCount    = `Rented Bike Count`, # Note the backticks for spaces!
    hour          = Hour,
    temperature   = `Temperature(°C)`,
    humidity      = `Humidity(%)`,
    windSpeed    = `Wind speed (m/s)`,
    visibility    = `Visibility (10m)`,         
    dewPoint      = `Dew point temperature(°C)`,
    solarRadiation= `Solar Radiation (MJ/m2)`,
    rainfall      = `Rainfall(mm)`,
    snowfall      = `Snowfall (cm)`,
    season        = Seasons,
    holiday       = Holiday,
    functDay      = `Functioning Day`
  )
```

There do not appear to be any missing variables, and season appears mostly uniform. We created some variables to help look at larger trends (months) and smaller trends (weekdays vs. weekends) in later analysis.

Then we summarized across the hours so that each day had one observation and value for all categorical/factor variables, and shows:
• sum of the bike_count, rainfall, and snowfall variables
• mean of all the other weather related variables.


```{r}
compressed_bikes <- clean_bikes |>
  group_by(date, season, holiday) |>
  summarize(
    across(c(bikeCount, rainfall, snowfall), sum, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(c(temperature, humidity, windSpeed, visibility, dewPoint, solarRadiation), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
```
Then we recreated our basic summary stats and then create some plots to explore relationships. 

```{r}

```

## Splitting the Data

We then split the data into a training and test sets.

```{r}
bike_split <- rsample::initial_split(compressed_bikes, prop = 3/4, strata = season)
	bike_train <- training(bike_split)
	bike_test <- testing(bike_split)
```

Our final bit of cleaning involved standardizing several of the numeric weather variables, then applying to both training and test datasets:

```{r}
bike_train_std <- bike_train %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(temperature, humidity, windSpeed, visibility, dewPoint, solarRadiation, rainfall, snowfall), 
      ~ (. - mean(.[dummy_var == TRUE], na.rm = TRUE)) / 
          sd(.[dummy_var == TRUE], na.rm = TRUE),     # Standardization
      .names = "{.col}_std"
    )
  )

Must port those std vars from train into test somehow.
bike_test_std
```
## Fitting a Model to the Data

fitting three different multiple linear regression models on the training data and predicting on the test set, reporting the RMSE
```{r}
reg1 <- lm(bikeCount ~ temperature_std + humidity_std + wind_speed_std + visability_std + dewPoint_std + solarRadiation_std + rainfall_std + snowfall_std + season + holiday + isWeekend, data = bike_train_std)
  #coef(reg1)
  #yardstick::rmse_vec(bike_train_std$???, predict(reg1))

reg2 <- lm(bikeCount ~ temperature_std:season + humidity_std + wind_speed_std + visability_std + dewPoint_std + solarRadiation_std + rainfall_std:season + snowfall_std + season:holiday + isWeekend, data = bike_train_std)
  #coef(reg2)
  #yardstick::rmse_vec(bike_train_std$???, predict(reg2))
  
reg3 <- lm(bikeCount ~ temperature_std:season + humidity_std + wind_speed_std + visability_std + dewPoint_std + solarRadiation_std + rainfall_std:season + snowfall_std + season:holiday + isWeekend + I(temperature_std^2) + I(humidity_std^2), data = bike_train_std)
  #coef(reg3)
  #yardstick::rmse_vec(bike_train_std$???, predict(reg3))

```

We then found the RMSE for each model against the test set:
  
```{r}
rmse_vec(bike_test_std$bikeCount, predict(reg1, newdata = bike_test_std))
rmse_vec(bike_test_std$bikeCount, predict(reg2, newdata = bike_test_std))
rmse_vec(bike_test_std$bikeCount, predict(reg3, newdata = bike_test_std))
  
```
